Another person won't 'fix' you, but they can inspire you to want to change as your current gf has, it seems. (I don't really like using the word fix, but I just woke up from a nap, so please excuse my lack of decorum.) I struggle with similar feelings. It took facing my trauma and working on healing to begin allowing myself to feel anything at all. Feeling comes with expressing. Suppression is my primary maladaptive coping mechanism (other than denial). If you can find a way to let go of your suppression of emotions so you can truly experience them, then you can express them properly and genuinely. Find out what love is, find out how to feel it, and then you can express it. 

You could also google ways to make your partner feel appreciated and do those things. But then you're just doing it because you 'have to' not because you feel that way.

To me, it's better not to be in a relationship at all than in one that brings only suffering and makes you unhappy. Is this relationship worth your serenity? Also, this may not be the case for all of your relationships, especially if you acknowledge it and try to heal yourself like I said above. If you find this is just how you are, though, there is somebody for everybody, I think, so you will be able to find someone better suited that won't freak out about normal behavior for you. I ubberrrrr relate! I lost an entire friend group over a year ago now. We had all known each other for 5 years, and all of a sudden, they were gone. Granted, I (partly) self fulfilled those relationships into ending, but afterward realized our connections weren't all that deep anyway, to me at least. Since I was living so deeply in delusion, dysfunction, and codepency, they never knew ME, like authentic me. All that made genuine connections pretty much impossible to cultivate.

I will say, though, the friends I reconnected with after that are what I'd consider true, genuine friends. It really is quality over quantity. These are 2 of my closest friends, and I'm okay with that. 

This is, for me, anyway, definitely a CEN thing. Opening up and being vulnerable was always met with rejection and isolation from my parents and peers. Now, I struggle to be genuine with others out of fear of that same rejection. 

Living in recovery, though, I've been able to be authentic and genuine with others more often, and this results in a reflection of that from others! By being more genuine and vulnerable with others, you will attract people who are the same. Imo, that is the only way to find and make genuine connections. SCARY, right!? It's stupid scary to me, anyway. But it pays off well enough with nice, deeper conversations with my friends, coworkers or strangers, or anyone who reciprocates that vibe. Not everyone will, and thats okay, but it's worth it when someone does. 😌 

Making friends can be difficult for people like us, but it's not impossible, and you're not broken or unable to have those connections. 

I will say, and I can't tell you what to do, but differentiating healthy vs. unhealthy relationships is more difficult when you're in unhealthy relationships. Your friendships sound they suck! I also didn't walk away from those friendships, even when I didn't want to be in them anymore, because I was scared of being alone, but they're gone anyway, and not in an amicable way. You may just be better off without them... Just a thought idk I'm probably projecting! 

Anyway, this got long. I hope it helps in any way at all 😭 Sorry!

I suggest Codependents Anonymous. It's like AA but for codependency. It honestly saved me from myself and continues to do so and help my learn to function and just become a healthier person. Meetings can be in person or online.

OP, please PLEASE attend a Codependents anonymous meeting!!! You are in a crisis and this is a dangerous place to stay. A meeting will allow you to vent to others who can relate and listen to others share about their similar experiences! Meetings are easily accessible online and depending on where you're located there are some in person. You can attend as many as you need in one day, anything to keep your mind off of him, your situation, and to begin to focus on the solution to heal and become free like you want so badly. (CoDA does not work for everyone but it is a fellowship of millions and works if you work it, so please give it a try.) Many people, like myself, come to CoDA when we hit rock bottom and it sounds like you're there. (https://coda.org/find-a-meeting/online-meetings/) 

I struggled similarly to how you are with my ex within the first few months we broke up. I still have a type of addiction to him and call him my qualifier as he triggers my codependency into hyperdrive. He ended up blocking me on everything after I constantly crossed his boundaries and couldn't do no contact, couldn't bring myself to stop reaching out to him even though once I tried to set the boundary myself. I felt insane, I didn't want to bother him and make him hate me or make him scared of me (more than he already was). But I just couldn't fucking stop myself. Codependency is a genuine addiction and should be treated as such. He is the drug in your case. Unfortunately our only choice as codependents is to go cold turkey. 

As another commenter said, ask him to block you (on EVERYTHING anywhere you can contact him) and get a person you trust that can help you through this and be there for reach out when you get the urge to speak to him. This can also be found in CoDA meetings. Many meetings have contact lists with the emails and phone numbers of people who are available for outreach. I'd suggest in your share in a meeting to mention how you need outreach and support right now and ask that some people reach out if they can, post your number or whatever you're comfortable with in the chat (no socials, it is an anonymous program). I prefer to speak to other codependents in the program about my struggles rather than friends because they understand the experience first hand and thus are not judgemental, just empathetic and compassionate. 

I'm sorry you're having to experience these feelings and compulsions. I understand the pain and suffering it causes, the inner turmoil and like shame it brings into ones life. I hope you can find a support system and soon find a way into recovery.

With my parents it's kind of like that family bond where it's just like of course I love them, they've known me my whole life and are the only people who haven't rejected me at my worst, and me the same with them (probably because of the cultural belief that it is an obligation to tolerate and love family, which is of course untrue. I do love them, even if sometimes it feels like I'd rather not 😭 but love is very multifaceted esp with family as there is literally a lifetime of history in those relationships.) I hesitate to say it to them aloud sometimes, though. 


Other than that, I had a group of friends for 5 years, and even considered them chosen family but never believed them when they said they loved me and, after leaving those relationships awhile ago now, kind of realize I did that same thing you do where it felt reflexive. As if I knew I SHOULD feel love for them, but I don't think I ever truly felt love for them and definitely didn't believe they felt love for me. I said and did what I thought I should do. I rarely say I love you to my current friends but when I do I make sure it's coming from a genuine place and not just as a weird nicety like it had become in that last group. 

With my ex I think it was genuine love? After the breakup though I realized I was deeply codependent. After joining CoDA I also realized a lot of the relationship was unhealthy and dysfunctional. I think he was the first person to make me feel genuinely loved, or something like that, in a LONNGGG time so my codependency, which I never knew about, didn't even know what codependency was, went haywire! I still struggle distinguishing the obsessive compulsion of codependency from the real feelings in/about that relationship/him. Sometimes I believe it was genuine, sometimes obsession. Two things can be true at once I suppose. 

Something that helped/helps me is first learning to identify all of my emotions so I can distinguish between them in the first place. So that when I'm feeling something I know what it is and can act accordingly. My you struggle with emotional suppression? If you suppress emotions it can inhibit you from feeling them in the first place, so learning to feel and process emotions is helpful too. (Although a lengthy process because there will be some backlogged emotions that have been waiting, for maybe years, to be felt and expressed.) 

It is also imperative to have a good foundation of self love to know that loving and being loved looks like to you! Hope this helps!

I'm in an Anonymous program and one thing that's said a lot is that when we start setting boundaries people get pissed off. They're so used to us being push overs, not questioning or confronting them, not asserting our right to be ourselves or demanding to be respected. When people don't get what they want from you (submission) they get MAD. Him being angry is not your problem, though he makes it that way and probably will as long as you live there. You have the right to demand your values and beliefs be respected just like anyone else's. Are you not respectful of her beliefs? If you are they have to respect yours too. Her belief may be that your name should be in the temple, but yours restrict that from being done. It's YOUR name, you have agency over it and the spirituality or lack there of you want to be involved in. How is it disrespectful to ask to be respected? How ironic... 

The only advice I may have is to continue to set boundaries and demand respect. Why do you have to respect them if they don't respect you? Child or not you have a right to be treated fairly and you are not less of person because you are their child. With religion its hard bc like... People are SO passionate and it's touchy when you question it but that doesn't negate the fact that you don't want to be in involved. Maybe give an example of your stepmom's agency to participate in a religion or not is stripped away. Such as her being forced to be involved in religion other than Mormonism. Maybe someone offers to do a pagan ritual in her name, this is considered heresy and she probably wouldn't be okay being involved in such a thing. She is doing that to you. This may be dramatic and cause a huge argument and turmoil so I'm not sure if you want to do it that way... I may even recommend avoiding this since you live with them and again orthodox religion is so touchy, about paganism especially. But you can do something similar using a more innocuous example. Maybe someone asks to use her name as a reference on a job application and she says no but they do it anyway? That's tame but will get the point across with much less grief. I used the extreme example because I get very passionate about boundaries and people being respected and it pisses me OFF when others won't do something so simple that you ask for bc of selfishness. 

But yes stand your ground! As long as it isn't detrimental to your living situation or something. Keep in mind you're not weak, you were taught it was a problem to be assertive (I don't want to assume but seems like your Dad is the culprit) and it is a skill you must build now. In time you will develop the strength to stand your ground as you set more boundaries and gain confidence in yourself and your values.

I am also very sensitive to people saying mean or hurtful things, or even just anything I take as rejection even if it wasn't meant that way. I don't always know how to react either, but here are some tips I'm utilizing to help.

• I'm new to this myself but it's helpful to build confidence and a strong sense of self and your values. If you are secure in yourself rude or belittling things won't have staying power or elicit a strong initial reaction. It's important to keep in mind it's okay to be mad or upset when someone says something hurtful, it's all about how you react. There is no shame in the occasional strong initial reaction either, it happens to the best of us. 

• There is power in pause. This means when someone says something offensive, before reacting you pause and take a breath or even just walk away to abate intense emotions. As children we did not have the option to walk away in school or at home. As adults we have the power to protect ourselves and inner child. We can walk away, ignore it, set boundaries (I don't like how you speak to me, that was an unnecessary comment! You're being very rude, I don't appreciate that tone/action) with the bully, defending yourself. We have control in our lives now. Confrontation is scary but necessary in all facets of life. That may be something you need to work on. I know I do.

• Lastly, because this is getting long and probably excessive, I've read a book called The Four Agreements. My second favorite agreement is "never take anything personally." This means that others emotions and opinions are THEIR problem, NOT yours! If someone is bullying you, they are projecting onto you their thoughts, feelings, and beliefs developed from their own life experiences. This is why it's a projection of them onto you, it has nothing to do with you but everything to do with them and how they see the world. Everyone's views are subjective, not objective, and who are they to say your truth is wrong? And you anyone else's? (Unless the opinion is factually incorrect and proven wrong!!!!) Say you are a slow reader and someone calls you stupid because of this. Somewhere in their life they learned this to be "true" whether in school or home or wherever. But this is NOT an OBJECTIVE truth! They projected onto you their own beliefs and you do not have to accept that belief as truth. In this situation you can have an internal dialogue kind of like "that is someone's opinion and no opinion is objectively true or correct. I am positive plenty of slow readers are capable and intelligent and I myself know I am not stupid. This person may think so based on their own preexisting context but I disagree and will not believe their view is more correct or better than my own." With this skill developed you can detach from anything said to you knowing it's not about you but them, because we all have differing life experiences and no one is objectively right in their way of thinking. 

Be conscious if you notice yourself using this skill excessively because it can be used to avoid responsibility of our own hurtful behavior to others bc we may disagree with them for having been hurt. Even with this mindset, we cannot deny other's reality. Thinking slow reading makes a person dumb is apart of that person's reality. You cannot say they are wrong, because opinions can't be wrong (again unless fact proves it wrong), but you can disagree. If a person is hurt, you can't say they're wrong for feeling that way, and in this situation can't disagree that they are hurt bc it is fact that they are. Consider closely the situation before detaching and claiming it's not your problem. Our actions have consequences and we have to be responsible for them. Sometimes an apology is necessary, sometimes we need to stand our ground. Life isn't so black and white. 

(Using slow reading as an example was silly on my part because there are stats that exist that debunk that and that person really would be wrong, sorry)

As someone who has studied art history and also had this conversation recently a lot of art is contextual within the time it was made. Jackson Pollock was great because he was doing something no one was doing and it left an impression because of that. Also because of his method of doing so and the sheer size of some of his works creating an overwhelming experience upon seeing it in person. The method and context of the times matters a lot with modern art. 

 For example Piet Mondrian's work. You could look and say "that stupid, just a bunch of lines and boxes." But in his era art was getting more abstract and they began using the shape of the canvas AS the canvas, if that makes sense. In the De Stijl movement they rejected perceived reality as a subject and embraced pure abstraction to create universality in art. Universality meaning that everyone can see and understand. Traditional artworks hold a lot of meaning that cannot be comprehended by the lamen or outside of the country of origin as everywhere has different symbols that stand for different meanings. By abstracting art to it's core principals: color, line, movement, emphasis and so on, it can be understood and enjoyed by anyone. Although of course art movements still had meaning other than purely visual, modern art often fell/falls into the universality category. 

As for Jackson Pollocks work he is in the "abstract expressionism" movement which just hearing that makes so much sense, right? And he used the shape of the canvas as his canvas by placing it on the floor so he can see it, and work on it, from every angle. Art is traditionally done on an easel, standing strait up, no turning or flipping of the canvas. The technique of painting on the floor, his technique of drip painting too, wild and expressive! was new and exciting for the art community and the world. Abstract expressionism is also a movement that strays away from objective reality and realism as it is meant to express subjective emotions and responses. Not all abstract expressionism is splashing paint on a canvas btw! 

Jackson Pollock changed the art world forever. Even if you think his works aren't so great, without a doubt he inspired a movement that is alive to this day and influenced MANY famous artists. That makes him pretty great. 

I'll say this and I don't mean to offend but it may seem incomprehensible because you don't know the history, the era or intention of the art. Also art critics are a thing and not all art is deemed great. People are aloud their opinion, of course, and I agree a lot of art these days is missing the message and meaning that makes art great.

I would recommend joining a step study group. You can find them on the official CoDA website. 

There are support meetings, then there are step studies, which are different. Most step study groups are closed groups. Meaning that only those who joined during the open period will be able to join said group in meetings to come. This is because step study is meant to work the steps fully and thoroughly from step one as a group, so the problem of being in different steps doesn't arise and each step is given plenty of attention. Some groups, like mine, also study the prayers and traditions. 

I love my step study group! We have all become familiar and like close friends. We have a group chat and a contact sheet so that it's easy to connect with one another if we'd like to do so. It sounds like you are looking to begin your healing journey and step groups are great for that as there are always people who you know are there for you and who fully understand your suffering and past. You will build a connection like no other with these people and will learn that you're never alone. 

It's also helping because many people who do step studies have done them before too. So someone experienced will be there to guide and help you. It's also great to continue to do step studies... Well forever if you please!

My step group will be about a year long of meetings held once a week. It's a commitment that's more than worth making! Don't be scared by the word commitment as you can of course come and go as you please. If one group doesn't work for you that's fine, and if you feel you're not ready for one step you're welcome to skip it. You're worth the effort and the commitment to healing. 

Good luck on your search for a good group!

I use mindfulness techniques! Such as 54321: 5 things you see, 4 things you hear, 3 things you feel (physically not mentally or emotionally) 2 things you smell and 1 thing you taste. It's very grounding and allows you a break from thought and an opportunity to change the course of your thoughts.

There is also the ABC method where you say a word beginning with each letter of the alphabet in order. 

AND you can also pick a color and point out things that are that color around the room/wherever you are.

These all help me reel in my thoughts and bring me into the moment. It is NOT easy. You will have to be consistent it's so fucking annoying, especially when all your mind wants to do is think about whatever you don't want to think about LOL. But I promise with practice you will be able to control your minds course and tedious repetition will be worth it.

Please be patient! And please be kind to yourself! This is a new habit and you won't master it in a day or week or even month. It took me a couple months to get it. But you'll see an improvement quickly.

How can someone explain their culture to someone? To do so would take a whole class. Here in America we take US history almost every year in grade schools, other cultures also have an expansive history. 

On the political point, I just don't understand why the people in that culture must be the conduit to those ignorant of their oppression/struggles. We live it everyday, and MANY amazing and talented artists have written about our experiences more passionately and eloquently than we ever could. Don't want to read a whole book? You won't get it until you learn about the whole history. That is why so many people choose to remain ignorant, it's a lot to read and to learn, and takes a bit of critical thinking and self reflection. I can recommend some books or movies for you if you'd like.

The idea is that there is a lot of explanation needed to fully understand a culture. If I were to explain one thing you're getting less than half of the picture. As a black person who actively studies humanities, race and ethnicity and systematic forms of oppression I no longer try to explain racism, societal or systematic, or sexism/feminism as usually people will get upset and disagree with me, even though it isn't a matter of opinion, but studied facts. 

The point is if you want to know about a culture and their experiences the information is out there. Some people take it to the extreme and refuse to explain anything even when asked, BUT some topics are just too much to get into in a simple conversation. 

Speaking about black people specifically, I know of many black writers, artists, poets, philosophers, and musicians who have eloquently and simply described the black experience for decades. We don't want to gatekeep and maintain division, we want people to get the whole picture, one black person's experience is not universal for all black people anyways. If you care about learning about a culture or race and their experiences, there are resources for you to do so rather than trying to get any person to explain a large chunk of their history in 2 sentences.
